passage: At the tea stall outside the kasba school, Devika bought a jalebi, a balloon, a packet of peanuts and a ribbon, all at once. Wasim watched, two rupees warm in his fist. Something pinched in his chest. He looked at Devika's shiny new pencil case and then at the corner of his own, cracked but neat. He remembered Abba's sewing machine humming late, and Ammi tucking a boiled egg into his bag that morning. Devika held out the jalebi. "Half?" Wasim hesitated, then broke off a piece. "Thanks," he said, and this time the pinch in his chest was small.

qa.q: How many rupees did Wasim have in his fist?
qa.a: He had two rupees in his fist.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling as he watched Devika buy things, and what helped it shrink?
qa.a: He felt a pinch of envy; remembering Abba's sewing machine and Ammi's boiled egg reminded him of what his own family gives, and the pinch grew small.

qa.q: How can Wasim cope when a friend has more pocket money?
qa.a: Remember that families differ and value what he has, instead of comparing, as he did.

qa.q: How might Devika see the moment at the stall?
qa.a: Devika probably had no idea Wasim felt a pinch; Devika was enjoying the treats and offered to share half of the jalebi.

grounding: Illustrates a child feeling envy at a friend's larger pocket money and settling it by remembering his own family's gifts.

passage: At the weekly haat in their village near Hisar, Kiran bought a toy car, a bag of jalebis and a shiny water bottle, all in ten minutes. His father worked in Dubai and sent money home every month. Vikas had four rupees in his pocket and a pang in his chest. He had never had a toy car that wasn't borrowed. Walking home past the mustard fields, he kicked a stone hard. Then Kiran said, 'Can you ask your Dadaji to help me make a kite like yours? Mine from the shop breaks every time.' Vikas thought of Dadaji's hands splitting bamboo and gluing paper, and of their kite that flew higher than anyone's. Families were different. His had something too. 'Come on Sunday,' he said. 'Bring the jalebis.'

qa.q: What did Kiran buy at the haat?
qa.a: A toy car, a bag of jalebis and a shiny water bottle.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling as he kicked the stone?
qa.a: Envious and a bit sad, with a pang that he had never had a toy car of his own.

qa.q: What helped Vikas let go of the comparison?
qa.a: Remembering that families differ and valuing what he has, like Dadaji's kite-making.

qa.q: How does Kiran see Vikas's family?
qa.a: As having something special, since Kiran wants Dadaji's help to make a strong kite.

grounding: A village boy feels a pang of envy at a friend's pocket money, then remembers families differ and values what he has.

passage: At school in Manchester, Jin always had money for the tuck shop: crisps, fizzy sweets, a new pack of trading cards every week. Kofi got three pounds a week and usually saved it. Watching Jin rip open yet another pack, Kofi felt a sharp pang. At home he grumbled, 'Jin gets loads more pocket money. It's not fair.' His mum was stitching a hem. 'Every family's different, Kofi. Jin's parents both work long hours, and he's with his childminder till seven.' Kofi hadn't known that. On Saturday morning he and his dad fixed the chain on his bike in the yard, laughing, oil on their hands. Afterwards he thought about Jin at the childminder's. Maybe he would invite Jin to fix bikes next Saturday.

qa.q: How much pocket money did Kofi get?
What was Kofi feeling as Jin ripped open another pack?
qa.a: Envious, with a sharp pang, feeling it was unfair.

qa.q: What helped Kofi value what he had?
qa.a: Mum reminding him that families differ, and his Saturday morning fixing the bike with Dad.

qa.q: What might Jin's weekdays be like, from what Mum said?
qa.a: Long, with his parents working late and Jin at the childminder's till seven.

grounding: A boy envious of a friend's bigger pocket money learns families differ and comes to value his own time with his father.
